activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Rowan wore his red team shirt. It was game day on the big court. His sister came to watch. She sat on the long bench with Mom.

Rowan bounced the ball. It came up small. He pushed it down soft. It came up small again.

"How do I make it go high?" Rowan asked.

"Push it down hard," his sister called.

Rowan pushed down hard. Up went the ball. It went high, high, high.

"Again," said Rowan. One hard push, one high bounce. Two hard pushes, two high bounces.

Coach blew the whistle. Rowan ran with the ball. He pushed it down hard all the way. Bounce, bounce, bounce. Then he stopped and shot. The ball went up and in.

The team cheered. Rowan bounced the ball one more time, just for fun.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Kinsley held her pink pig toy tight. Today was her first haircut at the mall. Mama said, "We can't be late for the salon."

The hairdresser put a big cape on Kinsley. "Snip, snip!" went the scissors. They were very loud. Kinsley hid her pig under the cape.

The scissors cut a little piece of hair. The hair fell down, down, down. It landed on the cape with a soft tap. Snip, snip. Another piece fell. Tap, tap.

"When the scissors cut, the hair falls down!" said Kinsley.

"That's right," said the hairdresser. She snipped some more. Soon the cape looked like it had snow on it. Grey snow, brown snow, little snow.

Kinsley lifted her pig up. "Pig, look at the snow!"

Then she shook the cape. All the hair bits fell off, down to the floor. The hairdresser swept them into a little pile.

Kinsley looked in the mirror. Her hair was short and neat. "Snip, snip, tap, tap," she said, and kissed her pig on the nose.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Penelope wants to make pancakes for her family. She stands on her step stool at the counter. Papa helps her pour the flour.

She stirs the milk and eggs. The batter is lumpy and smelly at first. "That's okay," says Papa. "Keep stirring."

Penelope stirs and stirs. The lumps go away. The batter turns smooth. One thing made another thing happen.

Papa puts the pan on the stove. Penelope stays back, because the stove is hot. Papa pours a small circle of batter. It bubbles all over.

"Look at that," says Penelope. The bubbles grow big. Papa flips the pancake. Now it is golden on top.

Her little brother, a boy named Sam, hangs on the gate and watches. "More," he says.

Papa stacks the pancakes on a blue plate. Penelope carries the plate to the table. Mama and Sam sit down.

Penelope passes out the forks. Everyone takes a big bite. "Yummy," says Sam, with syrup on his chin.

Penelope smiles. "I stirred it smooth," she says. Papa gives her a thumbs up.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Hunter turned four today. The party was at the big hall. There were balloons on the wall. Grandma had made a cake. It sat on the table.

But the candles were not lit yet. Hunter wanted to blow them out. That was his special job. He waited and waited. He tapped his shoes on the floor.

Dad came over with a long match. "Watch now," Dad said. Dad was careful with the match. He lit each little candle. One by one, small flames popped up. They danced and glowed.

Hunter stood close. The flames were warm. He did not touch them. Dad said, "Only my hands, Hunter. Flames can hurt." Hunter nodded and kept his hands back.

"Now blow," said Grandma. Hunter took a big breath. He blew hard. The flames all went out. Little smoke curls went up. Hunter laughed. He had done that! His breath had made the flames go away.

Mom brought a soft feather from the party bag. She touched it to Hunter's nose. It tickled. Hunter sneezed a tiny sneeze. Everyone clapped and sang the birthday song. Then Dad cut the cake with a careful hand. Hunter got the first big slice. He looked at his empty candles and smiled. "Again next year," he said.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Alexander dug a small hole in the dirt. He dropped in a seed and patted it down. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every day he looked at the spot. Nothing came up. Alexander felt sad. His grandpa said, "Try giving it a drink." So Alexander filled his watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Water ran down in little streams. A bird watched from the swing and clicked its tongue on the seed in its beak.

The next morning, something green stood in the dirt. It was small and new, like a tiny hand. "Grandpa, come see!" Alexander called. He poured more water on it, and the drops hung on the leaves. The little plant seemed to stand taller in the sun.

Iris looked in the toy box. She found a ball, a drum, and her robot. "Not Snow," she said. The robot blinked its lights, but no cat.

Next she went to the kitchen. Mom was there, wiping the table. Iris found an apple, some bread, and a banana. "Not Snow here either," she said. Her tummy made a little growl. Mom smiled. "You can eat the banana. Then keep looking."

Iris peeled the banana. It felt smooth and smelled sweet. She took a bite. Then she heard a soft sound. Pur, pur, pur.

The sound came from the laundry basket. Iris peeked in. Snow was curled up on a warm towel, fast asleep. "Found you!" Iris whispered. She petted Snow's soft fur. Snow purred even louder. Mom came over and said, "Shh, let the kitty nap." Iris sat down next to the basket and ate her banana, very quietly.

The duck went "Squeak, squeak!" Alexis jumped back. He was a little scared. Then he laughed. "The duck talks!" he said. The girl laughed too. Her face turned happy, like sunshine.

A boy ran by and grabbed the duck. "Mine!" he yelled. His face was red. He was angry. Alexis stamped his foot. But then the boy fell down, and the duck flew out of his hands. "Ouch," said the boy. He started to cry.

Alexis picked up the duck. He held it out. "You can share it," he said. The boy wiped his eyes. They sat on the cozy warm grass and counted ducks, one, two, three duck toys in a row. "Squeak!" said the duck, one more time.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Myles sat at the big art table. He wanted to paint a park. He had blue paint and yellow paint. But the grass was green. How could he make green?

He looked at his paper. He painted a blue sky first. Then he drew a red swing under a tree. He added a brown trunk. He stuck a furry pom-pom on for a dog. But the grass under the swing was still plain white.

Myles had an idea. He dipped his brush in blue. Then he dipped it in yellow too. He swirled the brush on the paper. What was that? The paint turned green! Green like real grass. He stared at the brush.

He painted and painted. Green grass went all around the swing. He pressed the furry pom-pom dog onto the green. A drop of green paint fell onto the table. "Miss Kim, look!" said Myles. "Blue and yellow made my grass!"

The teacher smiled and hung his painting up high. "Green park," said Myles. "My best one."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Jake sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He held his teddy bear on his lap. The nurse came in with a small tray.

"Will the shot hurt?" Jake asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said the nurse. "Then it is all done."

Jake's mom sat next to him. "You can squeeze teddy tight," she said. "Squeezing helps your hands stay busy."

"Okay," said Jake. "I will try that."

The nurse cleaned his arm with a soft white ball. It felt cold and wet. Then she got the little shot ready. Jake hugged teddy very tight.

"One, two, three, squeeze," said Mom.

"One, two, three, squeeze," said Jake. He squeezed teddy with all his fingers.

The nurse gave him the shot. It was one tiny pinch. Then it was over. Jake looked at his arm. "That was fast!" he said.

The nurse put a cute bandage on his arm. It had yellow ducks on it. Jake smiled at the ducks. Then he got a sticker, too.

At home, it was lunch time. Jake sat at the table with his fork. He used the fork to feed himself little bites of pasta. He fed teddy a pretend bite, too. "Teddy was brave," said Jake. "So was I."

Mom gave him a hug. "You did it," she said. "Next time will be easy, too."

Jake looked at his duck bandage. He patted it once, very softly.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Athena went to the store with Dad. Yesterday she had seen pink cupcakes there. She wanted one today. "The cupcake shelf is empty," said Dad. Athena frowned. Where did the cupcakes go?

The baker came out. "We sold them all yesterday," she said. "Bread needs to rest all night. So do cupcakes." Athena looked at the big bowl. The baker showed her the dough. It was puffy and soft. "Now it rests," said the baker. "Later it becomes cupcakes."

Athena wanted to see again. Dad said, "We can take the bus home now. We can come back tomorrow." Athena held Dad's hand. The bus was big and yellow. She looked out the window all the way home.

Tomorrow came after sleep. Athena put on her shoes. "Bus time!" she said. Dad laughed. They rode to the store. The shelf was full of pink cupcakes now. Athena picked the biggest one. She took a big bite. "The dough rested," she said. "And now it is a cupcake." Dad nodded and smiled. "Let's get one for Mom, too."

Daddy came over with a juice box. "Is the baby sleeping?" he asked. "Shh," said Ayla. Daddy tiptoed, big feet, slow slow steps. "Oops," he whispered. "Grandmas need quiet." Ayla put teddy on her lap. She rocked him side to side. "Hush, little teddy," she sang. The wind blew again. But this time teddy did not fall. The scarf held him tight. "Good blanket," said Ayla. activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The living room went dark. "Oh no," said Leo.

Dad came in with a candle. He lit it on the table. The flame stood up tall. The dark went away around it. Leo clapped his hands.

Then Mom brought more candles. She lit each one from the first candle. One flame touched another. That candle lit up too! "More light," said Leo. "Big light!"

Mom smiled. "We are a team tonight," she said. Leo sat on the rug. The candle flames tickled the dark with little dancing lights. His shadow jumped on the wall. He waved his hand. The shadow waved back!

"Can I light one?" asked Leo. "Not yet," said Dad. "Flames are hot. You watch, and I light." Leo watched the wick catch. Another light! The room got brighter.

"I hope the lights come back soon," said Mom. "Or not," said Dad. "This is fun." They ate crackers on the rug. Leo told a story about a candle that flew. The flames danced along. "Bedtime soon," said Mom. "No," said Leo. "Stay up with the candles!" Mom laughed. "Just a little, since it is a dark night." Leo leaned on Dad and watched the flames dance.

At play time, Zoey looked at her beautiful sweater. She found a Z in the zipper. "Zzzz," she said, and pulled it up and down. Sam laughed. Then he made his hands swim like fish. "F," he said. "Fff, fff, fish."

Sam nodded. "Look," he said, pointing at the door. "D for door."

Zoey ran to the window. "W!" she shouted. "Wuh, wuh, window!"

The teacher smiled and gave her a gold star sticker. Zoey stuck it on her sweater, right next to the zipper.

"Zzzz," she whispered, and gave the sticker a pat.

story:
Wren stood by the kitchen door. Her pink coat hung on the hook. Mom was making lunch at the counter. "Put on your coat," said Mom. "We will go out soon."

Wren pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm went in. The coat hung crooked, and the zipper end hung low. She pulled and pulled. The zipper would not start. The two sides were far apart.

Wren remembered the zipper trick. She sat down on the kitchen step. She pushed the zipper end into the slot. She held both sides close together. The zipper end made a little click. Then she pulled the zipper up, up, up. It worked! The coat was warm and snug.

"That is a pretty zipper," said Mom. "Ready for lunch in the park?" Wren nodded. She pushed the zipper down, then up again, all by herself. "Zip," she said. "Zip."

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Victor sat at the little table in the school library. He wanted to write his name on his paper. The teacher gave him a big red pencil. He held it in his whole fist, like a spoon. He pressed hard. The letter V came out all wobbly and fat. The i lost its dot. The dots ran away down the page.

Victor felt sad. "My name looks squished," he said. The teacher sat next to him. She showed him her hand. "Try pinchy fingers," she said. "Pinchy fingers," said Victor. He pinched the pencil near the tip, like a little crab. His fingers felt funny at first.

Then he made a V again. It was straight and tall. He made the i, and the dot stayed right on top. One letter, then the next. "Pinchy fingers," he whispered. At the end, he had a surprise. His name fit on the paper, and it looked like the name on his cubby at school. Victor washed his hands and carried his paper to show the teacher. "Look! It's me!" he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Charles went to the art studio with his grandma. He wanted to make a picture for his mom. He picked red paint and yellow paint. He also picked a big fat brush.

Charles painted a red circle. Then he painted a yellow circle. He wanted to make a red flower and a yellow flower. But the two circles touched each other. The paint began to mix. The red and yellow made orange where they touched.

Charles looked at his picture. "Oh no," he said. "My flowers are orange." He showed his grandma. She smiled and waited. Charles looked some more.

Then Charles got a new paper. He painted a red circle. He left a big white space next to it. Then he painted a yellow circle in the white space. He let the red dry first. The red stayed red. The yellow stayed yellow.

Charles looked at both papers. "Grandma, look!" he said. "This one is all orange. This one has red and yellow." Grandma helped him put a shiny sticker star on top. Charles carried his picture home very carefully with two hands. "For Mom," he said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Addison sat with Mom and Dad at a restaurant. A big screen showed a game. Everyone at the tables was watching it too.

Addison wanted to see the game up close. But the screen was far away. A tall man in front stood up. Now she could not see the ball at all. Addison stood on her tiptoes. Still no ball. Then Dad had an idea. He lifted her onto his lap. Now she was taller than the man. She could see the whole screen.

On the screen, a player kicked the ball. It went into the net. The net moved and the crowd jumped up. Addison clapped her hands. The people around her clapped too. Her cup was empty, so she took a smooth, cold sip of Dad's root beer. It helped fill her tummy with happy bubbles.

The waiter brought a warm plate of fries. Dad put some on her plate, because they were hot. Addison waved her little flag. On the screen, the players were smiling. "We won," she said softly. Mom kissed the top of her head.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Ibrahim sat at the art table. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to draw a house for his bear. But the bear had no house yet.

Ibrahim looked around the table. He saw a round lid. He traced around it. He made a circle! He held his paper up. "Look, a circle!" he yelled. His teacher smiled. "Nice circle," she said. "Now draw more shapes."

Ibrahim found a square block. He traced it. He made a square. He found a ruler. He traced it. He made a long rectangle. He picked up a brown crayon. He drew a triangle on top. "One circle, one square, one rectangle, one triangle," he said.

The circle became the sun. The square became the room. The rectangle became the door. The triangle became the roof. The house was done! But the door was too small for the bear. Ibrahim made a bigger rectangle. Now the bear fit right in. "Good night, bear," said Ibrahim. He laid the bear by the paper door.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
John was at Grandma's house. He wanted to go outside. The frogs by the pond were singing. They made a loud song.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. "But the zipper is hard," said John. Grandma smiled. "Try it yourself first."

John pushed his arms in. One arm went in the wrong hole. "Silly arm," said Grandma. John laughed and took his arm out. He found the right hole this time.

Now the zipper. John pinched the little tab. He pulled it up, up, up. But the coat had a bump inside. The zipper stopped. It would not go past the bump. John pulled and pulled. Then he smoothed the bump flat with his hand. He pulled the tab again. Zip! The zipper went all the way to the top!

"I did it!" said John. "Zipper up, frog song, let's go," said Grandma. They ran out to the pond. A fat frog sat on a rock. "Ribbit," it said, very loud. "He likes your coat," said Grandma. John patted his zipper. "Good zipper," said John. The frog jumped in with a splash.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Lena wants to draw a yellow sun. But the tablet is dark and still. She taps it. Nothing happens.

Her teacher, Mia, comes over. "Press the round button," says Mia. Lena presses the round button. The screen lights up. Lena smiles big.

She sees little pictures on the screen. One picture looks like crayons. Lena taps it. The crayon picture opens. Now she has colors to draw with. She picks yellow. She draws a big round sun. Then she draws a yellow flower too.

Mia reads a story to the other children. Lena wants to hear it too. She puts the tablet down on the shelf. The tablet goes to sleep, all dark again. Lena runs to sit with her friend Bo.

"Lena drew a sun!" says Bo. He saw her picture on the shelf. Lena nods and points at it. "It is yellow like my mom's phone case," she says.

Mia opens the book. Lena leans on Bo's arm. "Read the dog part," she whispers.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Paint day was here at school. Charlotte sat at the open table. She had red paint, yellow paint, and blue paint. Teacher Mia said, "Name your colours first." Charlotte pointed. "Red. Yellow. Blue." Then she had a want. She wanted to paint a big orange sun. But there was no orange paint on the table. "Where is the orange?" she asked. Teacher Mia smiled. "Try mixing two colours."

Charlotte put her brush in the red. She put it in the yellow. She stirred them together on her paper. The paint turned orange! Her sun was big and round and bright.

A boy named Sam ran over to look. "How did you do that?" he asked. Charlotte held up her brush. "Red and yellow made orange," she said. Then she dipped into blue and yellow too. Green swirls grew on her paper. Outside, a dog barked once, soft and happy. Charlotte painted on and on.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Jasper wanted his blue sock. It was lost somewhere. Yesterday he wore it. Today he could not find it.

Jasper looked under the bed. "No sock," he said. He looked in the toy box. "No sock." He looked behind the bear. "No sock."

"Keep looking," said Mom. "Now check the basket." Jasper looked in the basket. One sock, two socks, three socks. The third one was blue!

"I found it," said Jasper. He was sorry the sock had made him wait. "Tomorrow I can wear it," he said.

"Not tomorrow," said Mom. "Later today, after your nap." Jasper put the sock on his shelf. He patted it gently. "Wait here," he whispered. "I will come back soon."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Natalie sat in her playroom. She wanted to paint a frog. But frogs are green, and she had no green paint.

She looked at her paint cups. She had red paint. She had blue paint. She had yellow paint. No green anywhere.

"What makes green?" she wondered.

She dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She made a yellow dot on paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She painted right on the yellow dot.

The dot turned green!

Natalie leaned close. Her nose almost touched the paper. She saw the wet green spot. It grew bigger as she painted more.

She filled her brush again. More yellow. Then more blue. She made a big green frog with wide eyes.

"Mama, come see!" she called.

Mama came in and looked. "What a green frog," said Mama.

"I made green myself," said Natalie. She held up her wet painting. "Blue and yellow did it."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Lillian woke up from her nap. She wanted her bunny. Bunny was not in the bed. "Where are you, Bunny?" she said.

Lillian looked in one place. She looked under her little chair. No bunny. She looked in two places. She looked in her toy box. No bunny. She looked in three places. She looked behind the pillow. No bunny. Bunny was lost.

Then Lillian saw something. Her shirt was on the floor. The shirt was cold from the tile. Bunny liked soft, warm things. Bunny liked to sleep on soft things! Maybe Bunny was hiding under something soft. Lillian looked at her blanket. The blanket had a big lump in it.

She pulled the blanket back. There was Bunny! Bunny had made the blanket into a little hill. "Found you!" said Lillian. She hugged Bunny tight. Mommy came in and smiled. "Bunny was sleepy," said Lillian. She tucked Bunny back into bed. "Sleep now, Bunny." Bunny's soft ear flopped over, and Lillian patted it.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna jumped up and down. "One week, two weeks, no, one week!" she said. Grandma brought a big red truck full of her clothes. Sienna helped unpack. One shirt, two socks, three dresses. Then Grandma pulled out a soft wool sweater.

"I will wear it tomorrow," said Grandma.

The next morning, Grandma put on the sweater. "Oh dear," she said. "It is itchy." She scratched her arm. She scratched and scratched.

"Take it off!" said Sienna.

Grandma hung it over a chair. Sienna slid the chair next to Grandma. Grandma put the sweater on the chair. "Now my soft scarf can go on too," said Grandma. The chair stood there like a little coat rack.

"That is my chair!" laughed Grandma. "It holds my things."

Sienna ran to get her teddy bear. She put him on the chair too. "Four things, Grandma. Four!"

Grandma clapped her hands. Then she said, "Sienna, come here. Look what was in my truck." She held up a tiny sweater. "I made it for your teddy."

Sienna hugged Grandma and spun around. "Try it on! Try it on!" she said.
